rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all eight peaks while limiting late-elution risk. The retention window and critical resolutions will guide subsequent gradient and temperature adjustments.

Test a substantial temperature change at the same gradient to probe selectivity in the central cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room to slow the gradient afterward if needed.

Reduce the gradient slope substantially at the better-performing temperature to test separation of the remaining three critical pairs. The current early elution window suggests this can improve resolution without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The shallower gradient resolves the central cluster but introduces one near-coelution. Lower temperature by 5 °C to shift that pair's selectivity while preserving the favorable gradient and sub-10-minute elution window.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining central pair, while raising the initial organic fraction to offset the longer gradient's retention-time cost. The other pairs at 55 °C have useful resolution margins.

Raise temperature to improve the central pair, which responded strongly to temperature in earlier runs. The changed starting composition and slope may also separate the late pair that coeluted at 60 °C in injection 3.

Explore the cooler side of the selectivity crossover: the central pair may separate again after reversing order. This tests whether a lower-temperature region can resolve all pairs with the shallower gradient.
Test 35 °C to move beyond the close-pair crossings seen at 40 °C. Shorten the gradient to 24 minutes to offset increased retention and target a last peak before 10 minutes.

Probe the low-temperature endpoint to move away from the central coelution at 35 °C and assess an alternative selectivity region. A slightly shorter gradient should help keep the last peak near the 10-minute target.
Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF, so now test a two-minute shorter gradient for faster fully resolved elution. The minimum resolution of 1.89 provides some margin above the 1.5 requirement.

Reduce the endpoint organic fraction one step to give an effective slope between injections 9 and 10. This should recover the marginal central pair while retaining some of injection 10's time savings.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 11's slope to seek earlier elution without sacrificing full resolution. This tests starting-composition sensitivity, with injection 11 retained as the faster confirmed maximum-score method.

Slow the gradient at the higher starting organic fraction to recover the sole under-resolved pair. The 8.37-minute last peak leaves room for this adjustment while targeting full resolution before 10 minutes.

Shorten injection 13's gradient by one grid step to seek faster elution while retaining full resolution. The neighboring 20- and 24-minute runs suggest the critical pair may remain just above R = 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction to accelerate elution and use a shallower slope to compensate for its adverse effect on the critical central pair. This targets a faster fully resolved method than injection 14.

Lower the endpoint one step to recover resolution in the sole marginal pair from injection 15. This tests whether the higher-starting-organic method can achieve maximum CRF with a modest retention-time increase.

Test a 5 °C temperature increase on the fastest confirmed fully resolved method to seek earlier elution. This will establish whether its critical pairs tolerate warming; injection 14 remains the fallback.

Test warming injection 16, whose larger separation in the earlier central pair may better tolerate the selectivity shift observed at 30 °C. This could preserve full resolution while reducing the last retention time below injection 14's 8.90 minutes.

Test whether another 5 °C increase moves the marginal late pair through its selectivity crossing into adequate separation. The central pairs may also change order, so this probes a potentially faster fully resolved region rather than assuming resolution improves monotonically.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a substantially shallower gradient to rebalance the central and late critical pairs at 30 °C. The higher start should offset some of the longer gradient's retention cost; injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 18's initial gradient slope but switch to an earlier hold, targeting the unresolved last pair while leaving the resolved central peaks largely unchanged. The moderate endpoint may delay late elution, but the previous 8.01-minute window provides some time margin.

Return to the temperature that reliably gives full resolution and test a higher-start, shallower-gradient combination. The shallower slope targets the central pair, while the higher initial organic fraction may keep fully resolved elution faster than injection 14.

Preserve injection 16's successful slope but end the programmed gradient after 8 minutes, near the last peak's elution. This tests a shorter gradient program while aiming to retain full resolution and maximum CRF.

Use a slope slightly shallower than injection 14 to increase its narrow resolution margin while keeping elution near 9 minutes. The endpoint remains above the composition needed for the observed peaks, allowing a shorter programmed gradient without an early hold affecting separation.

Shorten injection 23's programmed gradient by two minutes while preserving its slope through the central critical pair. Test whether the earlier hold retains full resolution and sub-10-minute elution; injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.
